# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 2 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 2 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_002_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 1, Chapter 2

**1** After saying these things to me she fell silent, and I saw her no more. I was seized with trembling and grief, and I said to myself: "If even this sin is reckoned against me, how can I be saved? How shall I make amends to God for my many great and serious sins? With what words shall I ask the Lord to be merciful to me?" **2** While I was reasoning through these things in my heart, I saw before me a great white chair fashioned from the whitest wool, and there came an aged woman in shining garments, holding a book in her hands. She sat down alone and greeted me: "Greetings, Hermas." **3** I answered in grief and weeping, "Greetings, my lady." She said to me, "Why are you so gloomy, Hermas — you who are patient and good-tempered and always cheerful? Why is your face downcast and not radiant?" **4** I said to her, "It is on account of an excellent woman who says I have sinned against her." She replied, "Far be that from a servant of God! Nevertheless, the thought about her did arise in your heart. It is precisely such a thought that brings sin upon the servants of God. For it is an evil and ruinous intention when one who is righteous desires a wicked deed; and all the more so for Hermas, who is known for his self-restraint and abstinence from every evil desire." **5** "But it is not for this reason alone that God is displeased with you — it is also because you have not disciplined your household, which has sinned against the Lord and against you their parents. Although you are fond of your children, you have not admonished your household, but allowed it to fall into deep corruption. That is why the Lord is displeased with you. Yet he will restore all the past failures of your household, for by their sins and iniquities you have been worn away by the anxieties of this life. **6** But the great mercy of the Lord has taken pity on you and your house, and will strengthen and establish you in his glory. Only do not be idle — take courage and build up your household. For just as a smith works his piece by repeated blows, so the daily practice of righteousness will overcome all wickedness. Do not stop correcting your children; for I know that if they repent with their whole heart, they will be written in the books of life together with the saints."

---

### Council Notes

The elderly woman appears for the first time, seated on a chair of gleaming white wool — a throne of judgment but also of compassion. She will later be identified as the Church (ch 3-4).

The theology of this chapter is striking: Hermas's sin is internal desire (ch 1), but the greater issue is his failure as a father and household head. The pastoral concern for the Christian family is central.

The "books of life" (v. 6) connect to Revelation 20:12, 15; the image was common in Jewish apocalyptic. The blacksmith simile is one of the text's more memorable illustrations.
